lead.text: Another one. Moss closed a €30m Series C led by Portage at a valuation north of €1bn — Europe's newest unicorn on the day Sifted wrote it up, and Germany's newest on any reading. Ante Spittler and his three co-founders started in 2019 selling corporate cards to mid-market finance teams; the company now sits between those teams and every euro that leaves the business, with the receipt, the approval and the ERP line attached to each one. That is a boring, enormous job, and Berlin's fintech bench keeps producing companies willing to do it rather than chasing the consumer app. Moss is already in this register — its entry carries this round and the crossing it produced.

lead.text: NavVis raised €73.7m in a Series D led by the American private equity firm The Jordan Company, thirteen years after four researchers spun it out of the Technical University of Munich. It maps the inside of buildings — factories, plants, the mission-critical infrastructure nobody photographs — and keeps the digital copy synchronised with the physical one; Felix Reinshagen says customers trust it with billions of square metres of that data. This is the German pattern in a single line: a decade of unfashionable engineering, a growth round from abroad, and the company still headquartered in Munich.

lead.text: metr secured €10.5m in a Series B — energy and heating management sold into German housing stock, which is the least fashionable corner of climate software and the one with the most tonnes of CO2 sitting in it. It was a thin week for Germany: six of the roughly fifty European rounds Tech.eu tracked were German, and none of them was larger than €12m. Late July is when the country goes on holiday, and the funding calendar goes with it. A quiet week is not a verdict on the pipeline; it is a verdict on the month.

lead.text: 5U AI raised $3.2m in pre-seed funding led by London's Emerge Capital, a year after two Technical University of Munich graduates founded it. It builds digital workers for freight forwarding — quoting, bookings, shipment tracking, invoice reconciliation — and, unusually, records the reasoning behind each decision rather than only the outcome, so a freight team can audit why the machine did what it did. Munich keeps producing exactly this: industrial software sold to people who move physical things. It is the least hyped part of the German ecosystem and reliably one of the most durable.

lead.text: telli took €13.1m in seed money led by redalpine, with Cherry Ventures and Y Combinator following on, taking a two-year-old Berlin company past €16m raised in total. Its founders are betting that customer operations are one system pretending to be five — calls, CRMs, tickets, dashboards, each with its own queue and its own manual work behind it — and that AI belongs in the middle of that, running the operation rather than summarising it afterwards. It is a fat, unglamorous target, and unglamorous B2B software sold to people with real operational pain is precisely what Germany has been quietly good at for a decade.
